depth.building.name: Building
depth.building.see: One hall of an AI data centre: rows of racks, cold air in, hot air out.
depth.rack.name: Rack
depth.rack.see: One rack, two metres tall: servers, a network switch, power and cooling.
depth.board.name: Board
depth.board.see: One board: a large accelerator chip in the centre, with memory and power around it.
depth.chip.name: Chip
depth.chip.see: One chip, about two centimetres across: compute blocks, memory, and the pads that connect it outward.
depth.block.name: Block
depth.block.see: Inside one block, one working part of the chip: rows of small ready-made circuits called standard cells, and a grid of memory, joined by wires.
depth.gate.name: Gate
depth.gate.see: One logic gate: a tiny circuit that turns the ones and zeros on its inputs into one output, by a fixed rule. This one is four switches, drawn as the coloured layers they are made from.
depth.switch.name: Switch
depth.switch.see: One switch, called a transistor. In the newest chips, its gate wraps around thin sheets of silicon.
depth.atom.name: Atom
depth.atom.see: Silicon atoms in a crystal, with electrons moving between them.
stop.think.rack.q: An AI answers you from a rack like this. Where in here is the thinking?
stop.think.rack.note: Most of what you see moves power, heat and data. The sums happen in a few chips on each board.
stop.think.board.q: Chips on this board do the same simple sums side by side. Is thinking just a great deal of adding?
stop.think.board.note: An AI model is mostly multiply-and-add, repeated billions of times.
stop.think.chip.q: No block on this chip understands your question. So where does the understanding live?
stop.think.chip.note: Each block does one narrow job: add, store, or move numbers.
stop.think.block.q: A memory cell here is a loop that holds one bit. Is remembering part of thinking, or something separate?
stop.think.block.note: Join a pair of NOT gates in a ring, each feeding the other, and the pair holds whichever value it was last pushed into.
stop.think.gate.q: These switches make one kind of logic. Rewire the same switches and you get another. Does meaning come from the wiring?
stop.think.gate.note: Every logic gate on a chip is built from the same two kinds of switch. Only how many there are, and how they are joined, differs.
stop.think.switch.q: We use this switch in only two states: on and off. How can on and off mean anything at all?
stop.think.switch.note: The same group of switches can be read as a number, a letter or a colour; nothing in the switches says which.
stop.think.atom.q: Down here there are only electrons moving through a crystal. At which depth did the thinking begin?
stop.think.atom.note: Nothing at this depth knows it is part of a computer.
stop.strange.chip.q: Almost every chip is made of silicon. What else could a chip be made of, and what would change?
stop.strange.chip.note: Silicon won because it is cheap, can be made extremely pure, and grows its own insulating layer.
stop.strange.gate.q: Dominoes, water and beams of light can each build a logic gate. What makes something a computer?
stop.strange.gate.note: Two states are not enough. A gate's output must be strong enough to drive the next gates, or the signal fades along the way.
stop.strange.gate.tried: logic with droplets in tiny channels
logic built from strands of DNA
stop.strange.switch.q: What could replace the switch itself: a beam of light, an electron's spin, a living cell?
stop.strange.switch.note: Every candidate so far beats today's switch at something and loses at something else.
stop.strange.switch.tried: switches that use an electron's spin (spintronics)
stop.strange.atom.q: Could single atoms or molecules be the parts? What would we gain, and what would we lose?
stop.strange.atom.note: A working switch has been made around a single atom placed in silicon. It worked only at temperatures close to absolute zero.
stop.strange.atom.tried: switches built around a single atom
data stored in DNA, the molecule that holds a cell's instructions
stop.limit.rack.q: A rack like this can write, draw and compose. Is there anything it could never do?
stop.limit.rack.note: In 1936, before any chip existed, it was proved that some questions can never be settled by any machine.
stop.limit.chip.q: A chip is frozen the day it is made. What if it could keep changing?
stop.limit.chip.note: Most chips can never be rewired. A few kinds can.
stop.limit.chip.tried: chips that can be rewired after they are made
chips that learn while they run
stop.limit.gate.q: For some problems, the work doubles with every item you add. Is "too hard" a law of nature, or a lack of ideas?
stop.limit.gate.note: For such problems, a chip twice as fast only buys one more item.
stop.limit.gate.tried: settling for a good answer instead of the best
programs that rule out many cases at once
quantum computers, for a few special problems
stop.limit.atom.q: Physics sets a smallest energy for erasing one bit. Is there a floor under all thinking?
stop.limit.atom.note: Each time a switch in today's chips flips, it uses many thousands of times that minimum.
stop.fail.building.q: In a hall this size, something is always failing. Can a system be more reliable than its parts?
stop.fail.building.note: With hundreds of thousands of parts, rare faults happen every day.
stop.fail.board.q: One board here turns hundreds of watts into heat. Where does it all go?
stop.fail.board.note: Nearly all the electricity a chip uses leaves it as heat.
stop.fail.board.tried: chips that slow down when they get hot
stop.fail.chip.q: The design is exact. The arrival times are not. What does "on time" mean when every wire is a different length?
stop.fail.chip.note: If a signal arrives after the clock ticks, the chip reads the wrong value.
stop.fail.gate.q: No two of these gates come out identical. How do you design with parts you can't fully trust?
stop.fail.gate.note: Each is slightly faster or slower than its neighbour.
stop.fail.gate.tried: testing every chip and sorting by speed
sensors on the chip that adjust its voltage or clock
stop.fail.switch.q: A few atoms out of place change how this switch behaves. Is perfection even a meaningful goal?
stop.fail.switch.note: The thinnest layer here, the insulating skin, is only a few atoms thick.
stop.fail.atom.q: An insulating skin this thin lets electrons leak straight through. What do you do when the rules themselves change?
stop.fail.atom.note: At this size electrons behave partly like waves and can cross barriers that should stop them.
stop.idea.chip.q: Faster, cooler, smaller, cheaper: no chip gets all four. Who chose the trade-offs in this one?
stop.idea.chip.note: Every chip is a set of compromises made on purpose.
stop.idea.block.q: Nobody placed these cells by hand. If software arranged them, who is the designer?
stop.idea.block.note: People describe what the chip should do. Programs decide where most of the parts go.
stop.idea.block.tried: AI that places and wires chips
describing a chip in plain words
stop.idea.gate.q: The silicon of a chip can't be changed after it is made. How sure is sure enough?
stop.idea.gate.note: Teams often spend more effort checking a design than creating it.
stop.idea.gate.tried: simulating the chip before building it
stop.make.chip.q: Chips are printed with light onto flat round wafers. Was that the only way it could have gone?
stop.make.chip.note: The newest machines print with light of wavelength 13.5 nanometres.
stop.make.switch.q: This shape is made by adding layers and carving most of them away again. Could the whole shape grow by itself instead?
stop.make.switch.note: A modern chip takes a thousand steps or more to make, and every switch on the wafer, many billions of them, is made at the same time.
stop.make.atom.q: What if atoms could be placed one at a time?
stop.make.atom.note: It has been done in the laboratory, slowly, with the tip of a microscope.
stop.make.atom.tried: placing single atoms in silicon with a microscope tip, to build quantum computer chips
laying films down one layer of atoms at a time, already done in factories
molecules that arrange themselves into patterns
stop.know.chip.q: Two teams with the same tools get different chips. What does one know that the other doesn't?
stop.know.chip.note: Skill learned by doing is often impossible to put fully into words.
stop.know.switch.q: Getting this shape right took decades of trial and error. Can an AI learn what was never written down?
stop.know.switch.note: AI learns from recorded data. What was never recorded is the hard part.
stop.know.switch.tried: AI trained on factory sensor data
stop.open.chip.q: Many strangers can share one chip and split the cost. What should they build together?
stop.open.chip.note: Shared runs have put hundreds of small designs on one chip.
stop.open.block.q: An open block can be reused by anyone as a description, but its layout fits only one factory's process. What would let open chip parts spread the way open software did?
stop.open.block.note: Software grew this way: people building on each other's pieces.
stop.open.block.tried: open design kits: a factory's rules for drawing a chip, published
open RISC-V cores that anyone can reuse
shared chip runs that split the cost
stop.open.gate.q: An open design can be checked by anyone, and copied by anyone. Is that a strength or a risk?
stop.open.gate.note: For most chips, drawings like this one are secret: only the maker and its factory can check them.
stop.divide.building.q: Thousands of machines here act as one computer. Where does one computer end and the next begin?
stop.divide.building.note: A large AI model is trained across many racks at once.
stop.divide.rack.q: Most of this rack moves data and removes heat. Is that overhead, or is it the real work?
stop.divide.rack.note: Only a small part of the rack does the arithmetic.
stop.divide.board.q: A specialist chip sits at the centre with helpers all around. Who should be in charge?
stop.divide.board.note: The specialist is fast at one kind of sum and needs the others for everything else.
stop.divide.chip.q: A chip is a city of districts. What should be general, and what should be special?
stop.divide.chip.note: A general block can do any job passably. A special one does a single job far better.
stop.divide.chip.tried: chiplets: small chips joined in one package
stop.divide.block.q: Memory and logic sit apart, joined by busy wires. Was separating them a mistake?
stop.divide.block.note: Fetching a number can cost more energy than computing with it.
stop.divide.block.tried: stacking memory on top of logic
stop.life.building.q: A hall like this can use as much power as a town. A brain runs on about 20 watts. What is the brain doing differently?
stop.life.building.note: Much of a data centre's power ends up as heat that has to be carried away.
stop.life.block.q: Brain cells signal mostly when something changes. Chips already stop the clock to parts with nothing to do. What if a chip had no clock at all, and each part worked only when news arrived?
stop.life.block.note: Almost every chip marches to a clock. Designers stop it wherever a part is idle, yet the clock that is left still takes a large share of the chip's power.
stop.life.block.tried: brain-like chips that send a spike only when something changes
circuits with no clock at all
stopping the clock to idle parts
stop.life.switch.q: A synapse, the junction between two brain cells, stores and computes in the same place. What would a switch like that be?
stop.life.switch.note: In a brain, the connections that hold memories are the ones that do the computing.
stop.life.switch.tried: memristors: parts whose resistance remembers the current that has passed through them
stop.life.atom.q: Life builds with atoms cheaply, at room temperature. What could chemistry teach a factory?
stop.life.atom.note: A cell assembles complex molecular machines without a clean room.
stop.scale.building.q: Each answer costs less energy every year, yet we ask for ever more. Can the planet afford the answers we want?
stop.scale.building.note: Nearly all the electricity a hall like this uses leaves it as heat.
stop.scale.chip.q: Shrinking is slowing. What should double next: switches, usefulness, or something nobody measures yet?
stop.scale.chip.note: For decades the number of switches on the best chips doubled about every two years.
stop.scale.switch.q: Flat, then fins, then sheets. What comes after the sheet, and what happens when there is no next shape?
stop.scale.switch.note: Each new shape gave the gate a firmer grip on the channel, so the switch could shrink again.
stop.scale.switch.tried: stacking the two kinds of switch, one that turns on with a high gate voltage and one with a low, on top of each other
channels only a few atoms thick
stop.scale.atom.q: When a channel is a few dozen atoms long, what is left to shrink?
stop.scale.atom.note: The pattern of a silicon crystal repeats about every half a nanometre. A nanometre is a millionth of a millimetre.
depth.phone.name: Phone
depth.phone.see: A phone taken apart: the screen, the battery that has to last the day and fills most of it, and one small main board with the camera beside it.
depth.phoneboard.name: Board
depth.phoneboard.see: The phone's main board, a few centimetres across, packed with parts. There is no fan.
depth.soc.name: Chip
depth.soc.see: The phone's chip: processor cores, graphics, an AI unit and a camera unit, each in its own district.
depth.car.name: Car
depth.car.see: An electric car, roof and near side cut away: control units everywhere, joined by wires, with sensors looking out. The one in the footwell has its lid off.
depth.ecu.name: Control unit
depth.ecu.see: One control unit, the lid off: a small chip that decides, and big parts that switch real power.
depth.mcu.name: Chip
depth.mcu.see: A microcontroller, a few millimetres across: two small cores, the memory that keeps its program, and its links to the world.
stop.life.phone.q: Your brain runs all day on about the power of a dim light bulb. Your phone needs charging every night. What would a chip that sips, rather than gulps, look like?
stop.life.phone.note: Most of the time a phone's chip is waiting. How little it spends while waiting decides how long the battery lasts.
stop.life.phone.tried: Big and little cores: little ones for small jobs
Switching off every part not in use, many times a second
stop.divide.phone.q: Your phone answers some questions itself and sends others far away. Which work should stay in your hand?
stop.divide.phone.note: Phones now carry a unit made just for AI, so more of the thinking can happen without the network.
stop.divide.phone.tried: Small AI models that run on the phone
Splitting one task between the phone and the cloud
stop.know.phone.q: A phone photo is shaped by people who looked at thousands of pictures and said "that looks right". Can taste be written down?
stop.know.phone.note: The colours and tones a camera produces are tuned by eye, by teams who know what a good picture feels like.
stop.fail.phoneboard.q: All this is packed into a few square centimetres, with no fan. Where does the heat go?
stop.fail.phoneboard.note: When a phone gets too hot, it slows its own chip down to protect itself, and you.
stop.scale.phoneboard.q: Here the memory sits right on top of the processor. When you can't go smaller, do you go up?
stop.scale.phoneboard.note: Stacking shortens the distance data has to travel, which saves time and energy.
stop.open.phoneboard.q: The radio rules every phone follows are shared and public, yet only a few companies make the modem. Why?
stop.open.phoneboard.note: Writing a standard down is not the same as building something that works with every network in the world.
stop.divide.soc.q: This chip has a district just for photos and one just for AI. When does a job earn its own district?
stop.divide.soc.note: A special district costs space on the chip, and pays it back by doing its one job with far less energy.
stop.think.soc.q: Your camera finds faces before you press the button. Which part of this chip is doing that?
stop.think.soc.note: An AI unit does a great many small multiplications at once, spending very little energy on each.
stop.idea.soc.q: The processor cores here were probably designed by another company. Can a chip be built mostly from other people's blocks?
stop.idea.soc.note: Most phone chips combine licensed designs with parts their makers design themselves.
stop.idea.soc.tried: Licensing processor designs from one company
Open RISC-V designs anyone can use and change
stop.scale.soc.q: Phone chips are often the first made in each new factory process. Why phones?
stop.scale.soc.note: Phones sell in such numbers that they help pay for the newest, most expensive factories.
stop.fail.car.q: A car's chips must work in freezing winters and beside a hot engine, for many years. How do you design for weather you can't predict?
stop.fail.car.note: Car chips are tested at temperature extremes far beyond what a phone ever meets.
stop.divide.car.q: A car can have dozens of small computers, one for each job. Should it have a few big ones instead?
stop.divide.car.note: Every small computer brings its own wires, and wiring has become one of the heaviest parts of a car.
stop.know.car.q: A few years ago, car factories stopped because small, cheap chips ran out. How can a part that costs so little stop so much?
stop.know.car.note: Many car chips are made in older factory processes, in factories qualified years ago, which cannot simply be swapped.
stop.life.car.q: A car drives by watching through cameras and radar. Animals see with far less energy. What could chips learn from eyes?
stop.life.car.note: An eye does not send every point of light to the brain; much of the work happens before the signal leaves it.
stop.life.car.tried: Cameras that report only what changes, like an eye
Chips that compute right where the image is captured
stop.fail.ecu.q: This unit works the brakes. If one chip makes one wrong move, a life is at risk. How do you trust a chip with a life?
stop.fail.ecu.note: Safety chips assume that something will go wrong, and are built to notice it in time.
stop.fail.ecu.tried: Two cores running the same work in step, compared every moment
Self-tests every time the car starts
Safety standards that trace every requirement to a test
stop.open.ecu.q: Car makers often write their own software for chips they buy from others. What if the software were shared?
stop.open.ecu.note: More car makers now build on shared foundations, and compete on what they build on top.
stop.divide.ecu.q: The small chip decides; the big parts beside it switch the current. Where does thinking end and power begin?
stop.divide.ecu.note: Power parts are often made from different materials, such as silicon carbide, which handle high voltage and heat.
stop.think.mcu.q: This chip runs one small program, over and over, for the whole life of the car. Is that thinking?
stop.think.mcu.note: Most of the world's chips are small controllers like this one, not big processors.
stop.scale.mcu.q: This chip is made on purpose in an older process. When is smaller not better?
stop.scale.mcu.note: Memory that keeps its contents with the power off, like this flash, is hard to shrink, and older processes are proven over years.
stop.make.mcu.q: Chips like this are made by the billion and cost very little. What does it take to make something that cheap, that reliable?
stop.make.mcu.note: Making it cheap and making it reliable pull in different directions, and both have to win.
depth.scanner.name: Machine
depth.scanner.see: The machine that prints with light: light made from tin, bounced off mirrors and a mask onto the wafer.
depth.wafer.name: Wafer
depth.wafer.see: One wafer of your chips. Specks land at random, and every chip a speck touches is lost.
depth.die.name: Chip
depth.die.see: One of your chips, still on the wafer: test needles touch its pads before it is cut out.
stop.make.scanner.q: To get light short enough, this machine fires a laser at tiny drops of molten tin, over and over every second. Is this the simplest way to print a chip?
stop.make.scanner.note: Air swallows this light, so its whole path runs through a vacuum, bouncing off mirrors instead of passing through lenses.
stop.scale.scanner.q: Shorter light prints smaller details. What happens when the light can't get any shorter?
stop.scale.scanner.note: The newest machines gather the light with larger mirrors instead, to print finer still.
stop.scale.scanner.tried: Larger mirrors that gather more of the light
Printing one layer in several passes
stop.open.scanner.q: Every machine like this comes from a single maker. What does it mean when a whole industry depends on one machine?
stop.open.scanner.note: It took decades, and parts from many countries, to make it work.
stop.fail.wafer.q: Specks land at random. Why does a bigger chip come out broken more often?
stop.fail.wafer.note: A speck ruins only the chip it lands on, so the bigger each chip, the more each speck costs.
stop.make.wafer.q: Hundreds of square chips are made at once on a round disc. Why round?
stop.make.wafer.note: Wafers are sliced from a crystal that grows as a round rod, and the chips cut off at the edge are wasted.
stop.idea.die.q: This pattern began as someone's idea. How many people and machines did it pass through to get here?
stop.idea.die.note: Designing a chip for the newest process now costs more than most companies can spend.
stop.make.die.q: Next it is cut out, sealed in a package and wired to the world. Is the package becoming as important as the chip?
stop.make.die.note: Packages now join several chips and stacks of memory close enough to act almost as one.
stop.make.die.tried: Stacking chips on top of each other
Joining chips with light instead of wires
depth.crystal.name: Crystal
depth.crystal.see: Every chip starts as sand. It is purified, melted, and pulled up slowly as one perfect crystal.
depth.slice.name: Wafers
depth.slice.see: The crystal is sawn into thin discs and polished flatter than almost anything else people make. Here your wafer begins its journey.
depth.pkg.name: Package
depth.pkg.see: In another plant, the wafer is cut into chips. Each good one is placed on its package, often with memory beside it, and closed with a lid.
depth.ship.name: Out
depth.ship.see: A last test, then out into the world: into a data centre, a phone or a car.
stop.make.crystal.q: Every chip starts as sand, melted and pulled up as one perfect crystal. Why must the whole crystal be a single, unbroken pattern?
stop.make.crystal.note: A row of atoms out of place here would spoil every chip cut from that part of the crystal.
stop.know.crystal.q: Pulling a crystal this pure is slow and delicate. How much of it depends on people who have done it for years?
stop.know.crystal.note: Only a few companies in the world make most of the wafers chips are built on.
stop.strange.crystal.q: Silicon for chips is among the purest materials people make. Does it have to be?
stop.strange.crystal.note: Solar cells are made of silicon too, at a purity a chip could never work with.
stop.make.slice.q: A wire saw cuts the crystal into discs thinner than a coin. What is lost in every cut?
stop.make.slice.note: Much of the crystal turns to dust in the saw.
stop.scale.slice.q: Wafers grew from the size of a coin to the size of a dinner plate. Why stop there?
stop.scale.slice.note: A move to even larger wafers was planned for years, then shelved: every machine in every factory would have had to change.
stop.make.pkg.q: The chip is flipped face down and joined to its package by tiny solder bumps. Why face down?
stop.make.pkg.note: Face down, every part of the chip can connect straight to the package, not only its edges.
stop.divide.pkg.q: Here memory sits right beside the processor, in one package. Where should one chip end and the next begin?
stop.divide.pkg.note: Placing memory this close shortens the wires data has to travel.
stop.divide.pkg.tried: Stacking memory in towers beside the processor
Small chips side by side on a shared base, working as one
stop.fail.pkg.q: Chip and package warm up and grow by different amounts. How do you stop them tearing apart?
stop.fail.pkg.note: Materials are chosen to expand at nearly the same rate as the chip.
stop.fail.ship.q: Every packaged chip is tested once more before it leaves. Who decides what counts as good enough?
stop.fail.ship.note: Chips that run slower or hotter are often sold as a cheaper model instead of being thrown away.
stop.open.ship.q: The same factory makes chips for rival companies. What does a factory owe the companies it makes chips for?
stop.open.ship.note: Many chip companies design chips but never make them; a few factories make chips for all of them.
stop.divide.ship.q: One chip goes into a data centre, another into a phone, another into a car. Should they have been made differently from the start?
stop.divide.ship.note: Car chips are often made in older processes, phone chips in the newest, and data centre chips as large as a chip can be.
stop.make.clean.q: This whole factory exists to keep dust away from wafers. If we started today, would we still build it this way?
stop.make.clean.note: A speck far smaller than a hair can ruin a chip, so the air inside is kept far cleaner than an operating theatre's.
stop.make.clean.tried: Keeping only each wafer's sealed box clean, not the whole room
Small factories that fit in one room and make chips in small batches
stop.scale.clean.q: Each new factory for the newest chips costs more than the last. Can that cost keep rising faster than chips earn?
stop.scale.clean.note: Only a few companies in the world can still afford to build one.
stop.open.clean.q: Only a handful of companies can make the newest chips. What would change if making chips were as open as writing software?
stop.open.clean.note: Factories for older processes make chips for anyone who sends a design, and shared runs now cost about as much as a used car.
stop.know.etch.q: Robots carry the wafers, yet the factory depends on people who can tell when a machine is not quite right. Can that be written down?
stop.know.etch.note: Starting a new factory often means bringing in experienced people from an old one.
stop.fail.etch.q: Wafers are checked for flaws again and again along the way. How many checks are enough, when each one costs time?
stop.fail.etch.note: Catching a flaw early saves every step that would have come after it.
stop.divide.wires.q: Hundreds of machines each do one kind of step, and a wafer visits many of them many times. Who decides the order?
stop.divide.wires.note: Scheduling software routes every wafer, and one slow machine can hold up the whole factory.
stop.make.wires.q: Every layer goes round the same loop, and a chip needs dozens of layers. Must a chip be made one layer at a time?
stop.make.wires.note: One lap prints the pattern of a single layer; the wafer then goes back to cleaning for the next.
stop.fail.test.q: Needles test every chip before the wafer is cut. What can a test never catch?
stop.fail.test.note: A test checks only what someone thought to check.
stop.divide.test.q: Small chips come out good more often, as the map shows. Should one big chip be split into several small ones that work together?
stop.divide.test.note: Joining small chips in one package trades a little speed between them for many more good chips.
stop.divide.test.tried: Chiplets: several small chips side by side in one package
One giant chip that fills a whole wafer, built to work around its flaws
depth.clean.name: Clean
depth.clean.see: Into the factory. Before every layer, the wafer is washed until not a speck is left.
depth.deposit.name: Deposit
depth.deposit.see: A thin new film is laid over the whole wafer, from gases that react on its hot surface.
depth.print.name: Print
depth.print.see: Three machines joined as one: a light-sensitive layer is coated on, a pattern is printed into it with light, and the parts the light touched are washed away.
depth.etch.name: Etch
depth.etch.see: Plasma cuts the film away wherever the pattern left it uncovered, straight down.
depth.implant.name: Implant
depth.implant.see: Atoms of another element are shot into the silicon where it is open, then a flash of heat heals the crystal around them.
depth.wires.name: Wires
depth.wires.see: Copper fills the cut trenches and is polished flat. Then the wafer goes back round the loop for the next layer.
depth.test.name: Test
depth.test.see: Needles touch every chip on the wafer. The map shows which are good, which depends on your chip's size.
stop.idea.deposit.q: Some films are laid down one layer of atoms at a time. If we can build that precisely, what else could we build?
stop.idea.deposit.note: Two gases take turns, and each turn leaves exactly one layer of atoms.
stop.strange.deposit.q: Every layer here is a different material, chosen for one job: to conduct, to insulate, to block. Could a chip be built from entirely different materials?
stop.strange.deposit.note: Chips already use dozens of elements, far beyond silicon: copper, cobalt, tungsten, hafnium and more.
stop.fail.print.q: Each layer's pattern has to line up with the one below, to within a few atoms. What happens when it doesn't?
stop.fail.print.note: The machine measures the wafer's position again and again while it prints, and corrects it as it goes.
stop.scale.print.q: Printing is the slowest and costliest step, so whole factories are planned around it. What would change if printing were cheap?
stop.scale.print.note: Factories are laid out so the printing machines are never left waiting.
stop.make.etch.q: Plasma cuts trenches far deeper than they are wide, straight down. How do you cut only downward?
stop.make.etch.note: Charged particles are pulled straight down by an electric field, so they hit the bottom of the trench, not its walls.
stop.make.implant.q: Atoms of another element are fired into the silicon on purpose. Why would you want impurities?
stop.make.implant.note: A few added atoms change how easily current flows; that is what makes a switch possible.
stop.fail.implant.q: The beam knocks the crystal out of place; a flash of heat repairs it. How much damage can a crystal forgive?
stop.fail.implant.note: Heating for only a moment lets the atoms settle back into their pattern without the added ones wandering away.

depth.need.name: The job
depth.need.see: A chip is built from pieces. Here is what the community is building, a small open computer, and every piece it takes: built, open, or waiting for an engine that can check it. Pick a piece: it becomes your job.
depth.logic.name: Describe
depth.logic.see: Designers describe the circuit in text, one wire per line: what each output must be, made from the inputs with AND, OR, XOR and NOT. Beside it, the table of every answer the job wants.
depth.check.name: Check
depth.check.see: Before anything is built, the description is run against the job: every pattern of inputs goes in, and every answer is compared. A mistake found here costs minutes; found in silicon, months.
depth.gates.name: Gates
depth.gates.see: A program turns the description into gates from a library of small circuits called cells: AND, OR, XOR, inverters, flip-flops. The lit wires carry a 1 for the pattern shown.
depth.layout.name: Layout
depth.layout.see: The cells are placed in rows so their wires stay short, then joined by wires on two layers of metal, one running across and one up and down, with vias between them. Your design sits on one tile of a shared chip.
depth.masks.name: Masks
depth.masks.see: The layout is split into one stencil per layer: where the cells are, each layer of metal, the vias between. Each becomes a mask, which the factory's scanner prints onto the wafer, layer by layer.
stop.idea.need.q: Every chip starts as a job someone wrote down. Who decides what a chip should do, and what happens when the job changes after it is made?
stop.idea.need.note: A chip cannot be changed once made: a job written badly here is built into every copy.
stop.idea.need.tried: Specifications a program can check: the job written as properties every later step is tested against
Open specifications anyone may build to, such as RISC-V, a processor's list of commands free of licence fees
AI that drafts a specification and its tests from a job in plain words, for people to correct
stop.open.need.q: Could anyone design a chip? What would they need, apart from an idea?
stop.open.need.note: Open tools and shared chips have made a first design possible for one person; most of what it takes is still knowledge.
stop.divide.need.q: Should this job be a chip at all, or a program on a chip that already exists?
stop.divide.need.note: A circuit built for one job is faster and uses less energy; a program can be changed tomorrow.
stop.think.logic.q: Can a few lines of text describe a machine that will run billions of times a second?
stop.think.logic.note: Each line says what a wire must be, at every moment: the text describes a structure, not steps to follow one after another.
stop.think.logic.tried: Languages that generate the description from a program: Chisel, SpinalHDL, Amaranth
High-level synthesis: the job written in C++, the circuit chosen by a tool
AI that writes Verilog from a plain request, then has to pass the same checks as anyone
stop.know.logic.q: Who will read this description in ten years, when the chip is still running and its designers have moved on?
stop.know.logic.note: The text is the only full record of what the chip does: why each line is there often lives only in someone's head.
stop.fail.check.q: If every pattern you tried gave the right answer, is the design right?
stop.fail.check.note: Small circuits can be tried for every pattern; a processor has more than anyone could ever try, so checking means choosing which ones matter.
stop.fail.check.tried: Proofs instead of patterns for the riskiest blocks, with open tools such as SymbiYosys
Tests written in Python with cocotb, as Tiny Tapeout's templates do
Random patterns steered toward the cases no test has reached yet
stop.idea.check.q: An AI can now write a description like this in seconds. Who checks the AI, and with what?
stop.idea.check.note: The check does not care who wrote the text: it compares the answers. The hard part is saying exactly what the job is.
stop.idea.check.tried: AI assistants that write chip descriptions from a plain request
Formal verification: proving a design right for every input, without trying them all
Checks written by one AI and reviewed by another
stop.make.gates.q: A program turns your text into gates and chooses which cells to use. What is it trying to make small: the area, the delay or the energy?
stop.make.gates.note: The same job can be built from different cells; each choice trades one of these against the others.
stop.scale.gates.q: Your design needs a handful of gates. A phone's chip has billions. How can anyone design something that large?
stop.scale.gates.note: Nobody places them one by one: designers describe blocks, reuse proven ones, and leave the gates to programs.
stop.divide.layout.q: Thousands of cells, and every wire should be short. Where should each cell go?
stop.divide.layout.note: There are more ways to place them than atoms in the universe; programs shuffle cells and keep changes that shorten the wires, like a metal cooling slowly into order.
stop.open.layout.q: One person could never pay for a chip of their own. What changes when many small designs share one?
stop.open.layout.note: Shared runs split the cost of the masks and the wafers between everyone on them; open process kits let anyone see the rules.
stop.open.layout.tried: Tiny Tapeout: hundreds of small designs on one shared chip
Open process design kits from SkyWater, GlobalFoundries and IHP
OpenROAD and OpenLane: open tools from description to layout
stop.scale.masks.q: Each newer process needs more masks, and each set costs more. Who can still afford to make a chip on the newest one?
stop.scale.masks.note: A mask set is paid once, before the first chip works: the more copies are made, the less each one carries.
stop.make.masks.q: The masks are made larger than the chip and shrunk onto it by light. Why not draw the chip directly onto each wafer?
stop.make.masks.note: Drawing with a beam is possible, but far too slow for millions of chips; a mask prints a whole chip at once.
stop.fail.gates.q: Every answer is right. Will it be right in time, before the next tick of the clock?
stop.fail.gates.note: Each gate takes a moment to answer, and the longest chain of gates between two flip-flops sets the shortest tick a chip can run at. A design can give every right answer and still fail at the speed it was meant for: no check of its answers would show it.
stop.fail.gates.tried: Timing every path at every corner of the process, slow and fast, hot and cold, as OpenSTA does inside OpenROAD
Cutting a long chain in two with flip-flops between (a pipeline): shorter ticks, but an answer takes more of them
Logic without a clock, each part saying when it is done: hard to design and check, so still rare
stop.fail.layout.q: Your wires join the right cells. Can the factory print them as they are drawn?
stop.fail.layout.note: A factory can print only some shapes: too thin and a line breaks, too close and two lines run together. It writes its limits down as design rules, and a program checks every shape against them before any mask is made.
stop.fail.layout.tried: Public rules: SKY130's and GF180's are open, checked by open programs such as Magic and KLayout
Every line on a fixed grid, one direction per layer, at the newest processes, so fewer shapes can go wrong
Dummy metal added where a layer is too empty, so polishing leaves the wafer flat
stop.idea.masks.q: Your layout is finished. What does it take to turn it into a chip you can hold, and who can do that today?
stop.idea.masks.note: Sending the final layout to be made into masks is called tapeout; after it, every mistake costs a new set. On SKY130 the factory prints 34 masks, and a shared run puts many designs on one chip so each pays a small share: one Tiny Tapeout chip carried 273.
stop.idea.masks.tried: Tiny Tapeout: a template, the open flow run for every design, a tile on a shared chip and a board it comes back on, six to nine months later
A whole run for one small group: about 1,000 chips of your own on GF180, from wafer.space
Keeping the path open when a company closes: after Efabless shut in 2025, shared runs moved to IHP, SkyWater and GlobalFoundries
design.proj.half.d: Adds two bits: 0 + 0, 0 + 1, 1 + 0 and 1 + 1. The first building block of every calculator and processor. Its description is already right: follow it through.
design.proj.vote.d: Spacecraft run three copies of a computer and trust the answer at least two agree on. The output is 1 when two or more inputs are 1. The description has a bug: the check will find it.
design.proj.full.d: Adds three bits: a, b and the carry from the column to the right. Chain them and you can add numbers of any size. The sum line has a bug.
design.proj.add2.d: Adds two numbers from 0 to 3 by chaining a half adder and a full adder, as processors chain them for 64-bit numbers.
design.proj.seg.d: Turns a number from 0 to 7 into the seven segments of a digital display, as in clocks and ovens. Segments a, b and c are done; d to g are left at 0.
design.proj.alu.t: ALU slice for a RISC-V core
design.proj.alu.d: One bit of a processor's arithmetic and logic unit. A RISC-V core copies it 32 times, each carry feeding the next. op1 op0 picks the job: 00 AND, 01 OR, 10 XOR, 11 ADD, and with sub = 1, ADD becomes SUBTRACT. Only AND is done.
design.proj.free.d: No job written down: four inputs, two outputs, any logic you like. The check shows what your circuit does instead of judging it.
design.proj.count.d: Counts from 0 to 7 and round again, one step per clock tick while en is 1. It must remember where it is, so it needs flip-flops: write reg in front of a line. The carry into the top bit has a bug.
build.need.computer.d: A small open computer on one shared chip, around a RISC-V core: designed piece by piece by many people, and by AI with them.
build.need.core.d: The processor: it reads instructions written in RISC-V, an open instruction set anyone may use, and does what they say.
build.need.alu.d: Adds, subtracts and compares: 32 copies of one slice, each passing its carry to the next.
build.need.slice.d: One bit of the arithmetic unit. Get it right once, and the core uses it 32 times.
build.need.adder2.d: Two adders chained: the way a carry ripples from one bit to the next.
build.need.full.d: Adds three bits; it sits inside every slice.
build.need.half.d: Adds two bits: the smallest piece of all.
build.need.regs.d: The 32 places the core keeps the numbers it works on: 1,024 register bits, and a select that says which register to write.
build.need.decode.d: Reads each instruction and sets every part of the core for it. Needs an engine that understands instructions.
build.need.timer.d: Counts clock ticks, so programs can measure time.
build.need.display.d: Shows a number on a seven-segment display.
build.need.safety.d: Runs three copies of an answer and keeps the one at least two agree on.
build.need.check.d: Catches a flipped bit with a parity check.
build.need.serial.d: Talks to the outside world one bit at a time. Needs an engine that understands timing on a wire.
build.aiUse.you: No AI: I wrote it myself.
build.aiUse.ai: An AI wrote it; I checked it in the lab.
build.aiUse.both: An AI wrote a first draft; I changed it and checked it in the lab.
design.proj.parity.d: Lights when an odd number of the four inputs are 1: memories store this extra bit to catch one that flips. One input is missing from the description.
design.proj.core.d: A processor that runs real RISC-V programs. Its arithmetic unit is your ALU slice, copied 32 times, each carry feeding the next; its registers are made of your register bit and register select once you have written them. Its decoder and memory are the lab's model for now. Its description here is a program to run on it.
design.proj.regbit.d: One bit of a register: it keeps its value, and takes the new value d only on a clock tick when we (write enable) is 1. The core's registers are 1,024 of these. The description takes d at every tick, write or not.
design.proj.select.d: Picks which register to write: s1 s0 is its number, and exactly that output turns on, but only while en is 1. The description forgets en.
build.need.bits.d: 32 registers of 32 bits: one register bit, copied 1,024 times.
build.need.regbit.d: One flip-flop that keeps its bit, and takes a new one only when told to.
build.need.select.d: Turns a register's number into the one wire that lets it be written.

map.quarry.d: Every chip starts as sand, purified and grown into one perfect crystal, then sliced into wafers. It is the first part of making.
map.studio.d: The first stop of a chip's life: a job, a description of what the chip should do, a check, then gates, a layout and masks. The mask house sends finished designs down the road to the factory.
map.fab.d: In a cleanroom, wafers go round the machines dozens of times for months, one layer per lap: printing, etching, filling.
map.datacentre.d: Halls of racks where AI is trained and answers questions. Fly inside, down to a single chip.
map.port.d: Chips are packaged and shipped across many borders. Each chip's next life depends on where it goes: a phone, a car, a data centre.
map.cars.d: Dozens of small computers in every car, built to last for years in heat and cold.
place.aria: Inside the place: scroll or drag to go deeper
map.test.d: Every chip is tested before it leaves, with a few patterns chosen to catch the most faults in the least time.
map.lab.d: A chip starts here, with something still open. The community is building one small computer, people and AI together, and every piece built adds a floor to this tower.
map.village.d: Every house is a design someone gave to the shared computer: a person, an AI, both, or a program. A design that passed its test can still be broken, and a tower marks each case that did it. Empty plots wait for a design.
map.phones.d: Billions of phones, each with a chip that must be cheap, cool and quick, and live a few years in a pocket.
map.idea.d: A sandbank for what this world does not have yet: a stake for every question nobody can try yet, and room for a place, a challenge or a question you propose.
map.plot.engine: This piece needs an engine to check it first
game.ch.half.goal: Fix the half adder so it adds two bits right.
game.ch.half.why: Every chip starts as a description of what it should do. A computer turns it into gates and wires, so a mistake here is copied into every chip made.
game.ch.vote.goal: Fix the majority voter that spacecraft trust.
game.ch.vote.why: An AI will offer a fix here, and sound sure about it. The check decides, not the confidence.
game.ch.full.goal: Fix the sum line of the full adder.
game.ch.full.why: Chain full adders and you can add numbers of any size. One wrong row, and every sum that passes through it can be wrong.
game.ch.months.why: A wafer goes round the factory's machines dozens of times, one layer per lap. A factory running full earns the most, and makes every wafer wait.
game.ch.quick.t: A chip that is quick to make
game.ch.quick.why: Some chips are needed fast: a first test chip, a part for a car line that has stopped. Fewer layers mean fewer laps.
game.ch.spot.goal: Run a few test patterns and find the copy the factory broke.
game.ch.spot.why: One speck of dust can break a wire. Nobody can try every input on every chip, so testers choose the patterns that catch the most faults.
game.ch.cores.why: A wafer in a newer process costs about one and a half times as much, so shrinking no longer makes each switch cheaper. A bigger chip holds more cores, but one flaw throws more of it away.
game.ch.phone.goal: Choose what the design and the factory do, so a phone's chip lives through its years.
game.ch.phone.why: A phone is cheap, warm in a pocket and replaced after a few years. What it needs is not what a car needs.
game.ch.car.goal: Make a car's chip last for years in heat and cold, with failures counted in parts per million.
game.ch.car.why: A car carries hundreds of chips, and one that fails can stop it on the road. Car makers ask for almost none to fail.
game.ch.dclife.goal: Keep a data centre's chips right while they run flat out and hot, with no silent errors.
game.ch.dclife.why: In a fleet this big, something that happens to one chip once in a lifetime happens every day, and a wrong answer nobody notices is worse than a crash.
game.ch.fed.why: A chip computes fast, then waits for numbers to arrive from memory. Moving data costs more time and energy than computing with it.
game.ch.fast.why: For decades chips got much faster every generation. Now a generation buys about an eighth more speed, and the slowest signal and the heat set the limit.
chipx.aria: A cut through a chip, layer by layer: scroll or drag to move through the layers
board.aria: One server board in 3D: tap a part to bring it into the story, drag to turn the board
dive.aria: The flat dive inside a chip, from the chip down to its atoms: scroll or use the arrow keys to go deeper, tap a part to name it
game.ch.piece.goal: Pick a piece of the community's computer and say what it must answer, three patterns in a row.
game.ch.piece.why: A chip starts as a job: these inputs in, these answers out, every time. Before anyone draws a gate, someone has to know exactly what is wanted.
game.ch.thousand.goal: Of a thousand designs that all pass every check, choose one, and write in one line what you chose it for.
game.ch.thousand.why: Programs, and now AI, can make more designs that pass every check than any team could ever look at. What is left is the question no check answers: which one, and for whom? Who uses it, who repairs it, who pays, what it costs the planet, what it must never do. The choice, and its reason, may be the part only people can give.
game.ch.floor.goal: Place the 2-bit adder's cells so the wires joining them are as short as the placer's.
game.ch.floor.why: Wire is not free: every step of it is delay, energy and room. With seven cells you can do it by hand; a real chip has billions, and programs place them.
game.ch.maskof.goal: Say which mask each shape of your layout is printed from, five right in a row.
game.ch.maskof.why: The factory never sees your description, only the masks: one stencil per layer, each shape on exactly one of them.

loop.logK: What you met, what you did, what waits
loop.mapK: The chip world on one page: every place and level, where you have been, and your log

break.lead: Untrue, confusing, broken, or could be better: say so, here and now. It goes into the lab's open record, signed, and calls for a fix until someone makes one. Nobody has to ask you first.
break.ph: What is wrong, or what would be better? 10 to 400 plain characters.
break.none: Nothing reported here yet. You could be the first.

exp.think-nand.ask: Can one kind of gate build every other?
exp.think-slice.ask: Your one-bit slice, copied 32 times, runs real programs. Where did the arithmetic come from?
exp.think-seven.ask: A tiny network tells a 7 from a 1 by adding. At which level is the 7?
exp.think-count.ask: How many switch flips make one sum? How many make one sentence from an AI?
exp.think-add-down.ask: Follow one add from the program down to the electrons. At which depth is the adding?
exp.strange-domino.ask: Dominoes can add. What can they not do twice?
exp.strange-chain.ask: Pass a 1 through ten gates. In which materials is it still a 1 at the end?
exp.strange-neurons.ask: A computer made of living neurons is on sale. Is it a computer?
exp.strange-for.ask: Here is a switch that is slow, tiny and never forgets. What is it for?
exp.strange-score.ask: Each new way beats today's switch at something and loses at something. At what?
exp.limit-floor.ask: How far is your chip from the least energy physics allows for one step?
exp.limit-cold.ask: Cool the chip and the floor drops. Why does that save nothing?
exp.limit-fell.ask: This wall was called final in its day. What moved it?
exp.limit-all.ask: To be sure of a 64-bit adder you would try every input. How long would that take?
exp.limit-evolve.ask: A blind search found a circuit that works and nobody can explain. Would you ship it?
exp.fail-margin.ask: How much speed do you give away to be safe from the worst chip in a million?
exp.fail-phone.ask: Choose what the design and the factory do so a phone's chip lives through its years.
exp.fail-cases.ask: Seven real chips passed their checks and failed. What did each check not know?
exp.fail-leak.ask: A chip that computed every answer right leaked secrets through its timing. Is correct the wrong word?
exp.idea-one-char.ask: Change one character of the description. Which form of the design notices?
exp.idea-two-ways.ask: Two descriptions give the same answers. Are they the same chip?
exp.idea-masks.ask: From a few lines to a set of masks: what did each step add that you never said?
exp.idea-coverage.ask: Your tests catch most of the faults a factory could leave. What are the others?
exp.idea-afford.ask: Your design fits one tile of a shared chip. What would it cost to make it alone?
exp.make-quick.ask: Make a chip that needs fewer layers and still has its cores.
exp.make-months.ask: Get your wafers through the factory in under 60 days while it runs nearly full.
exp.make-round.ask: Hundreds of square chips on a round disc. What does the rim cost?
exp.make-order.ask: Fire the atoms in before the gate is made, or after. Which order lines itself up?
exp.know-copy.ask: A second factory, the same machines, worse chips. Copy everything, or learn again?
exp.know-laser.ask: Nobody built this laser from the papers alone. What was missing from the papers?
exp.know-handover.ask: Write down what you learned. Can someone else reach your result from your note alone?
exp.know-tune.ask: Nine dials, some unlabelled. Get the etch right without being told how.
exp.know-agent.ask: A search program turns the same dials. What does it know when it is done?
exp.open-cents.ask: A 32-bit RISC-V chip now costs less than ten cents. What becomes possible?
exp.open-kit.ask: An open design moves to another factory. What has to be done again?
exp.open-stops.ask: Close one place on the map. What stops, and where?
exp.open-split.ask: One set of masks, a thousand strangers. What does each one pay?
exp.open-shuttle.ask: Could this record become a real chip on a real shared run?
exp.divide-fed.ask: Get two and a half times the work done, with every signal on time.
exp.divide-xray.ask: Read a chip from its photo: where its area goes says what it is for.
exp.divide-cores.ask: More cores, still cheap: where is the limit?
exp.divide-industry.ask: One company designs, another makes, a third packages. Is the industry a floor plan too?
exp.life-damage.ask: Kill a tenth of the parts. Which machine still answers?
exp.life-trail.ask: Nobody is in charge of this lab. What pulls work to where it is needed?
exp.life-rule.ask: Change the rule that says which open thing calls loudest. Does the lab organize itself better?
exp.scale-rules.ask: Shrink every length by the same factor. For thirty years speed and power followed. What broke the rule?
exp.scale-curve.ask: Fifty years of doubling on one line. Where does it bend?
exp.scale-forecast.ask: The lab keeps dated forecasts from its sources, checked every month. Which ones will hold?

game.ch.cheaper.goal: Make a chip with at least 64 million parts, where each part costs no more than a quarter above the cheapest part this factory can make.
game.ch.cheaper.why: More parts on one chip spread the cost of a wafer over more parts, until the chip is so big that a speck of dust lands on most copies. A cleaner line kills fewer, but every wafer costs more.
game.ch.oxen.goal: Build one chip that runs an everyday app at least 10 times and trains an AI at least 150 times as fast as one small core, using no more than 256 units of chip.
game.ch.oxen.why: Seymour Cray asked whether you would plough a field with two strong oxen or a thousand chickens. A strong core is quick at steps that must come one after another; many small cores are quick at work that can be split.
game.ch.onebad.t: The pieces' bet: one big chip or many small ones
game.ch.onebad.goal: Make a big chip, 600 mm² of logic, so that each working chip costs at most half as much as one big untested piece, with at least 9 in 10 packages working.
game.ch.onebad.why: Big chips are now often split into pieces (chiplets) joined in one package. A small piece comes out good more often than a big one, but a package works only if every piece in it is good.
game.ch.prove.t: The proof's bet: test it, or prove it?
game.ch.prove.goal: Check a chip of eight blocks so that the chance any bug ships is at most 1 in 100, spending at most 20 on random tests and proofs together.
game.ch.prove.why: Random tests are cheap, but a bug that shows once in ten billion inputs needs tens of billions of them. A proof by machine covers every input of a block at once, but it costs more, most of all for blocks full of control and memory.
game.ch.jevons.t: Jevons' bet: does a better chip save energy?
game.ch.jevons.goal: Let the world get at least 8 times as many answers as today, on less power than today: at most nine tenths of what the island's 13 turbines make now.
game.ch.jevons.why: Each better chip makes an answer cheaper, and when answers get cheaper people find more to ask. Whether the energy falls depends on which grows faster: the saving in each answer, or the asking.
game.ch.agent.goal: An AI agent makes eight proposals: designs, programs, an estimate, a claim. Check each with the lab's own tools, then trust the sound ones and reject the flawed ones for their real flaw.
game.ch.agent.why: Agents now write designs, code and answers that read well and are often right. Who signs off when one is wrong? Some of these are right, so rejecting everything does not win.
game.ch.cim.goal: Let a grid of memory cells do the multiplying, and find the cheapest converter that keeps its sums within 5% of exact.
game.ch.cim.why: Fetching a number from memory can cost more energy than computing with it. Computing where the numbers are stored saves the trip, but the sums are analog: currents that vary, read by converters that cost more with every bit.
game.ch.spikes.goal: Tune a spiking neuron so it fires on its own pattern at least 3 times and never on anything else, then count its work against a clocked circuit's.
game.ch.spikes.why: A brain spends energy mostly when something happens: a neuron that hears nothing sends nothing. Most chips march to a clock and work out every input on every tick, news or not. Spiking chips copy the brain's habit, and the question is when it pays.
game.ch.light.goal: Steer light through an interferometer so it multiplies by a quarter, then add phase noise until it stops being exact: exact on 90% of passes, and not at one step more.
game.ch.light.why: Moving numbers between chips already goes by light. Light can also compute on the way: split, delayed and joined again, it multiplies as it passes, with no clock. But a phase is a tiny delay, and heat moves it.
game.ch.grover.goal: A prize hides in one of eight boxes. Grow the chance of finding it as far as it goes, then take one more step. What happens?
game.ch.grover.why: A quantum search finds one thing among many in far fewer steps than opening the boxes one by one. But every step has to be clean, and the search has to stop at the right moment.
game.ch.batch.t: The batch bet: fast for one, or busy for many?
game.ch.batch.goal: Serve a 70-billion-weight model on one 2026 AI chip so that each person gets at least 200 words a second, and the chip's arithmetic is busy at least 80% of the time.
game.ch.batch.why: For every word it writes, the chip reads all 70 billion weights from memory and does only two sums with each. Serving one person, it mostly waits; serving many at once, each read is shared, until the sums fill up and everyone waits on everyone else.
game.ch.newest.t: Look inside: how many need the newest fab?
game.ch.newest.goal: Open five products, a phone, a car, a thermostat, a laptop and an AI server, and count the kinds of chips that need a leading-edge factory.
game.ch.newest.why: The newest factories make the famous processors. Everything else inside a product, most of its chips, comes from older, cheaper factories and other materials.
game.ch.jobs.t: The right chip for the job
game.ch.jobs.goal: Eight real jobs, and a line of chips from one that runs anything to one that does a single job efficiently. Find the best fit for each.
game.ch.jobs.why: A chip that can run anything pays for its freedom in energy and speed; one built for a single job is far more efficient at it, and useless at anything else.
game.ch.evolve.t: Evolve a circuit: beat the person
game.ch.evolve.goal: Let blind evolution search for a majority voter, y = 1 when at least two of three inputs are 1, that needs fewer cells than the person's design.
game.ch.evolve.why: Design is a search through a huge space of possible circuits. People search with reasons; evolution with nothing but copies, small random changes and a test. As AI starts to design chips, what do machine-found designs look like, and can anyone say why they work?
game.ch.crystal.goal: Pull a 300 mm silicon crystal from the melt with no dislocations, and taper it off before lifting it out.
game.ch.crystal.why: Every chip starts as a slice of one crystal, grown from a seed dipped in molten silicon at about 1,420 °C. One flaw carried in from the seed, or a jolt when the crystal leaves the melt, spoils what follows.
game.ch.furnace.goal: Implant boron at 2 keV, then compare a furnace anneal with a laser anneal. How much deeper does the furnace drive the junction?
game.ch.furnace.why: Dopants are atoms that change how silicon conducts. Firing them in damages the crystal, so the wafer is heated to repair it and switch them on, and heat also lets them wander. How hot, and for how long, decides how sharp a transistor can be.
game.ch.shallow.goal: The next transistors need junctions only a few nanometers deep. Make an n-type junction shallower than 15 nm with more than 95% of its dopants switched on.
game.ch.shallow.why: The source and drain of a tiny transistor are thin doped pockets. If the dopants sink too deep, the switch leaks; if too few switch on, it is slow.
game.ch.vias.goal: With no shift, find the largest random error that leaves at most one failed via per chip. Then see what a 2 nm shift does.
game.ch.vias.why: Every layer of a chip is printed on top of the last. A via is a tiny metal pillar joining a wire in one layer to a wire in the next, and a chip has ten billion of them. One that misses its wire breaks the chip.
game.ch.etch.goal: Etch a hole with less than 5 nm of undercut while keeping at least 70% of the mask.
game.ch.etch.why: Wires and gates are cut into films by etching. If the cut spreads sideways under the mask, the part ends up the wrong size, and at a few nanometers wide there is no room for that.
game.ch.bottom.goal: Deepen the trench until CVD leaves its bottom with less than 5% of the film on top, then coat it evenly with ALD. What does an even coat cost in time?
game.ch.bottom.why: Before wires are cut, deep narrow trenches must be lined with thin films. A film that stops short of the bottom leaves a hole in the part, so the way a film is grown matters as much as what it is made of.
game.ch.litho-finest.goal: Find the finest lines each scanner can print: from the old mercury lamp to the newest EUV machine.
game.ch.litho-finest.why: Printing draws every layer of a chip with light, so the smallest line the light can draw sets how small a chip can be. Each new kind of scanner (shorter light, a wider lens, cleverer tricks) bought a few years of smaller chips.
game.ch.euv-1000.goal: Turn the EUV light source up to 1,000 W and reach 275 wafers an hour. Can this scanner get to the 330 an hour that ASML aims for by 2030?
game.ch.euv-1000.why: EUV light is so weak by the time it reaches the wafer that the machine's speed, and so the price of every chip, depends on how much light the source makes and how little is lost on the way.
game.ch.too-hot.goal: Heat pure silicon until its own free electrons are as many as lightly doped silicon has: a million billion in every cm³. At what temperature does the doping stop deciding how a chip behaves?
game.ch.too-hot.why: A switch works because a few added atoms decide where silicon conducts and where it does not. Heat frees electrons everywhere, whatever was added. Somewhere there is a temperature where the heat wins.
game.ch.transistor.goal: Make a switch that really turns off, one that spends less energy than today's silicon fin, one steeper than 60 mV per tenfold, and a better one a factory could make.
game.ch.transistor.why: Every chip is one kind of switch, billions of times over, and silicon has won for sixty years. Below about 60 mV per tenfold no switch that works over a barrier can turn on at room temperature, which is why chips' voltages stopped falling. Where is the way past it?
game.ch.ai-chip.goal: Pick a brief and be the architect. Tape out a chip that meets every line of it.
game.ch.ai-chip.why: No choice moves one number alone. A bigger die is faster and yields worse; faster memory lifts speed and the bill; a newer process saves power and costs months. What each step of the lab taught comes back here as a trade-off.
game.ch.power-curve.goal: This chip starts at 3 GHz and 0.75 V, and takes about 51 W. Find the fastest clock that runs safely on less than half that power: 2.2 GHz or more, under 25.5 W.
game.ch.power-curve.why: Every switch that flips takes a sip of energy, and the sip grows with the square of the voltage. But a lower voltage makes the gates slower, so the clock has to slow down with it. That trade is why a chip cannot simply be run faster, and why every chip has to choose its place on a curve like this one.
game.ch.counter.goal: Clock a four-bit counter at the top speed its slowest path allows, with no wrong count, at two different processes. Then push on, and watch it break.
game.ch.counter.why: A tick of the clock is a promise: every signal will have arrived before the next tick. The longest chain of gates between two flip-flops decides how short a tick can be. No two gates come out identical, so designers add up the worst case and keep a margin. How much speed is that margin worth?
game.ch.sig-heart.t: A heartbeat on a coin cell
game.ch.sig-heart.goal: Catch a clean heartbeat for under 20 µW. Which part of the chain eats the budget?
game.ch.sig-heart.why: A phone, a watch or a patch on the skin only knows the world through chips like these: a tiny voltage is made bigger, measured many times a second and turned into numbers. Every number has to be kept or sent, and that costs energy.
game.ch.sig-bearing.goal: Sample a motor's vibration too slowly and watch the warning tone vanish; find the slowest rate that keeps it.
game.ch.sig-bearing.why: A car listens to its own parts. A bearing that starts to fail adds a faint, fast tone to the motor's hum. A chip that measures too rarely does not just miss it: it reports a slower wave that was never there.
game.ch.reg-jobs.goal: Find the best power supply for a fitness band, a phone processor, a precise sensor and a radio.
game.ch.reg-jobs.why: No chip runs straight from a battery. A power chip stands between them and holds the voltage steady while the load jumps. How it does that decides how long the battery lasts, how hot the board gets and how clean the supply is.
game.ch.quantize.goal: With at least 1 weight in 100 an outlier, fit a 70-billion-weight model in under 40 GB, and keep the signal more than 20 dB above the rounding error.
game.ch.quantize.why: What a language model knows is held in its weights: 70 billion numbers here, and every word it writes means reading all of them from memory. Storing each in 4 bits instead of 16 makes the model a quarter the size, but 4 bits can tell only 15 values apart. What is lost depends on how the weights are spread.
game.ch.token-energy.goal: First see the building at its best: with the chip untouched, bring cooling and the rest of the server under a fifth of an answer's energy. Then get an answer down to half the energy it started with.
game.ch.token-energy.why: A model writes its answer in tokens, pieces of words. Each token costs energy at the AI chip, and more around it: power supplies, fans, the network, and the cooling that carries the heat away. Which of these is worth working on depends on where the energy really goes.
game.ch.prefill.goal: On one Rubin chip with a 70-billion-weight model, find how long a prompt must be before reading it takes as long as writing a 270-token answer.
game.ch.prefill.why: A language model reads your prompt in one pass, all its tokens (pieces of words) side by side. It writes its answer one token at a time, and each token needs a pass through every weight. So a long question can cost less time than a short answer.

Chips have grown faster much more quickly than memory has, so a faster chip waits more of its time for data.

game.ch.flaky.t: Six flaky parts, one reliable chip
game.ch.flaky.goal: Build each block of a small chip once, three times or five times with a voter, so the whole chip goes wrong fewer than 5 times in 100 runs, on no more than 32 units of floor.
game.ch.flaky.why: In 1956 John von Neumann asked how a machine can be more reliable than the parts it is made of. One answer: make copies and take the majority. A vote outlasts any one bad copy, but copies cost area and power, and the voter is a part too. Space probes and the safety chips in cars still vote today.
game.ch.mortal.t: Learn on one chip, copy to a thousand
game.ch.mortal.goal: Make a network at most 30% as costly per answer as an all-digital one, right at least 95% of the time on its first chip, and at least 90% on every copy.
game.ch.mortal.why: A brain computes with very little energy because what it learned is the physical state of its own cells, and so it cannot be copied. A digital computer copies perfectly, and pays to move every bit. Chips that compute with analog cells sit between the two: cheaper, but each chip is a little different. Geoffrey Hinton calls computing whose knowledge dies with its hardware "mortal".
game.ch.noise.goal: Factor 15 with p-bits: right at least 90% of the time, with the shortest wait that does it, for less energy than trying every pair.
game.ch.noise.why: Switches are now so small that heat makes them flicker, and chips spend a great deal of energy holding each one still. A p-bit turns this around: it is built to flicker, and wired to lean on its neighbours. Many of them together search for answers by themselves, and some hard problems are found faster by noise than by trying every case.
game.ch.noise-big.t: A bigger number, the same noise
game.ch.noise-big.goal: Factor 143 with p-bits: right at least 90% of the time, with the shortest wait that does it, for at most a third of the energy of trying every pair.
game.ch.noise-big.why: Each bit added to the numbers doubles the pairs an exact search must try. A network of p-bits does not try pairs one by one; it settles, and how long that takes grows far more slowly. On small problems the plain search is fine; on large ones the difference is the whole point.
game.ch.dieread.goal: Say what kind of chip each die photo comes from, four times, and find every kind of block on one die by its texture alone.
game.ch.dieread.why: Engineers read die photos to learn what a chip is for, check what they were sold, and find where a chip failed. Memory, logic, repeated cores and hand-drawn circuits each have a look under the microscope, and where the area goes gives the chip's purpose away. Trusting a chip starts with being able to see inside it.
game.ch.silent.goal: Protect a chip at the levels where it can be protected, so that in a phone, a car and a data centre in turn it gives few enough silent wrong answers, without costing more area and energy than the place allows.
game.ch.silent.why: Every part of a chip goes wrong now and then: a particle flips a bit, a signal arrives late, a copy is born broken. Most wrong values are fixed, caught or shrugged off; the dangerous ones are silent. A protection catches only what it can see: a code on memory never sees a wrong sum, and copies of the logic all read the same wrong word. So the question is not how much protection, but which, and where.
game.ch.rvrun.goal: Write three small programs for the community's RISC-V core, each checked by running it on every case.
game.ch.rvrun.why: A processor only ever does a few simple things: add two numbers, compare them, jump to another line, move a number in or out of memory. RISC-V is an open set of those instructions that anyone may build a processor for. Everything a computer does is a long list of such steps, run a few billion times a second.
game.ch.search.t: Design it, or search for it?
game.ch.search.goal: Find how much computing a blind search needs to beat a person's design. Then let the checker try only half the inputs, and see what the search finds.
game.ch.search.why: In 2019 the AI researcher Rich Sutton called it the bitter lesson: again and again, methods that use more computing have beaten methods built on human cleverness. Here the cleverness is a person's circuit, and the computing is a search that tries circuit after circuit and keeps the best. It works only because every circuit can be checked.
game.ch.halt.goal: Build one gate from dominoes, water or light, and a bit that remembers. Then fool an agent that claims it can tell whether any program will stop.
game.ch.halt.why: A computer is a pattern, not a material: anything that can make one simple gate can, given enough of them, compute anything. Yet in 1936, before any computer was built, Alan Turing proved there is a question no computer can always answer: will this program ever stop?
game.ch.ear.goal: The picture is hidden. Listen to the block, slowed down a billion times, and say what it is doing: busy, waiting on memory, too hot, or saving power. Get eight right of your last ten.
game.ch.ear.why: A chip works far too fast to see or hear: billions of steps a second. Slowed down until each step is a sound, its state can be told by ear, the way a mechanic hears what is wrong with an engine. Training your ear for it is learning a new sense for a world too fast to see.
game.ch.corearch.goal: Make the core at least twice as fast on the puzzles' programs, in no more than 1.4 times its area, for no more energy.
game.ch.corearch.why: Every core is a trade: a part that makes some programs faster costs area on the chip, and energy every cycle it is powered, whether it is used or not. Architects choose the parts that earn their place for the work the chip will do.

game.ch.reversible.goal: Build an adder from Toffoli gates, then find the fastest steps at which it loses 100 times less energy than switching at once.
game.ch.reversible.why: Ordinary logic throws bits away at every gate, and physics charges heat for every bit erased. Logic that can run backwards erases nothing, so in principle it can compute for almost no energy, if it is willing to go slowly. As switches near their limits, some people are building chips this way.
game.ch.dataflow.t: Keep the numbers on the chip
game.ch.dataflow.goal: Lay a model's layers across a chip's tiles, and find the largest model the chip holds whole: one layer more must not fit.
game.ch.dataflow.why: Moving a number costs far more energy than computing with it. A processor fetches a model's weights from memory again for every answer; a dataflow chip keeps them in its tiles, where the work happens. It saves the most, until the model no longer fits.
